readerTitle: Why Costco won't touch its $1.50 hot dog
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Costco 푸드코트 핫도그 세트) + 일화 (Sinegal·Jelinek) + 실제 연구 (가격 이미지) + 가상 적용 (팀 채팅 소프트웨어)
insight: 고객이 기억하는 몇 개의 가격이 사업 전체가 비싼지 싼지를 알려주는 표지판 역할을 한다. 그 가격은 한 품목의 마진보다 더 큰 것을 지킨다.
misconception: 모든 상품은 각자 마진을 남겨야 하고, 원가가 오르면 모든 가격을 똑같이 올리면 된다.

sources.text: Costco food court hot dog and soda combo at $1.50 since 1985: Costco investor materials and widespread news coverage (e.g., CNBC, Seattle Times)
Former CEO Craig Jelinek recounting Jim Sinegal's reaction to raising the hot dog price: news coverage from 2018
Costco press release (2024) on membership fee increase, and Costco Form 10-K filings on membership fee income
Hamilton, R. & Chernev, A. (2013). Low Prices Are Just the Beginning: Price Image in Retail Management. Journal of Marketing.
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI-U (for the inflation adjustment)

factChecks.note: 핫도그+음료 세트가 1985년부터 $1.50라는 점, 게시 시점에도 여전히 $1.50인지 Costco 자료와 최신 보도로 다시 확인하세요.
Sinegal이 가격 인상을 막았다는 일화는 2018년 Jelinek 발언 보도에 근거합니다. 원문 인용은 쓰지 않고 "colorful threat"로 바꿔 말했으며, 일화라는 점을 카드에 밝혔습니다. 보도 원문을 확인하세요.
공급사 변경, 탄산음료 브랜드 교체(Coca-Cola→Pepsi, 2010년대 초로 보도), 자체 핫도그 생산(2009년경으로 보도)은 언론 보도 기준입니다. 연도는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다. 확인 후 유지하세요.
핫도그 세트의 실제 수익성은 Costco가 공개하지 않았습니다. 카드에는 "many observers assume"로만 적었습니다.
미국 기본 회원비 $60→$65 인상(2024년 9월 시행)과 회원비가 영업이익의 큰 부분을 차지한다는 점은 Costco 보도자료와 10-K로 확인하세요.
Hamilton & Chernev(2013) 인용 정보와, 가격 이미지가 평균 가격만으로 정해지지 않는다는 요약이 원문과 맞는지 확인하세요.
푸드코트가 출구 근처에 있다는 설명은 일반적 관찰이며 매장마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 "often"으로 적었습니다.

cards.title: The price that never moved
body: In 1985, Costco's food court began selling a hot dog and a soda for $1.50. Adjusted for inflation, that's more than $4 today.
Beef, buns, wages and rent have all become more expensive since then. The combo still costs **$1.50**.

image.label: A hot dog and soda under a $1.50 sign, with a calendar flipping through decades
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 창고형 매장 푸드코트 카운터 위에 핫도그와 음료 컵, 뒤편에 "$1.50" 가격판. 옆에 1985부터 최근 연도까지 넘어가는 달력. 가격판만 그대로. 실제 Costco 로고, Kirkland 상표, 음료 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Costs have been rising for years.
body: You run Costco's food court. The hot dog and soda combo has cost $1.50 for a long time, and what it costs you to make keeps rising. The food court is a tiny part of a huge business.

options.text: Raise it to $1.99. It's still a bargain.
options.feedback: Honest and simple, and it covers costs. But you'd be changing the one Costco price nearly every shopper knows, and they might start wondering what else went up.

options.text: Keep $1.50 and work hard to cut what it costs to make
options.feedback: You give up easy margin and take on harder work behind the counter. In return, the store's most famous price keeps telling shoppers they're getting a fair deal.

options.text: Keep $1.50 but quietly serve a smaller hot dog
options.feedback: The price stays, but regulars spot a shrunken signature item fast. It sends the same message as a price rise, and it adds the feeling of being tricked.

cards.title: Costco kept the price and changed everything behind it.
body: Over the years, Costco reportedly changed suppliers, switched soda brands and started making its own hot dogs. Those steps helped hold costs down without touching the price.

There's also a well-known story. Former CEO Craig Jelinek has said that when he raised the idea of a higher price, co-founder Jim Sinegal answered with a colorful threat and told him to figure it out. It's an anecdote, retold many times.
Costco hasn't published what the combo earns. Many observers assume it makes little or nothing.

cards.title: Price image
body: **Price image** is the overall impression customers have of how expensive a business is.

Shoppers can't remember hundreds of prices. So they judge the whole store from a few prices they *do* know. Researchers who study price image find that it isn't simply the average of all your prices. A handful of visible, memorable prices can carry a lot of weight.
The hot dog may be the most memorable price in any Costco.

image.label: Many price tags fading out while one hot dog price stays bright
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 매장 선반에 흐릿한 가격표 수십 개, 그 사이에서 "$1.50" 핫도그 가격표 하나만 선명하게 빛남. 가격표에서 쇼핑객 머릿속 말풍선 "This place is a good deal"로 화살표. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Why a hot dog makes a good signpost
body: Not every cheap price shapes how customers see you. This one has four traits that help.
list: **Easy to compare:** everyone knows roughly what a hot dog costs at a stadium
**Bought often:** many members grab one on a regular trip
**Seen at the end:** the food court is often near the exits, so it's the last price of the visit
**Unchanged:** a price frozen for decades becomes a story people repeat for free

cards.title: Every business has a few signpost prices.
body: Grocers often watch the prices of items shoppers know well, like milk, eggs or bananas, more closely than the rest of the shelf.
Signposts can work against you, too. A hotel guest may forget the room rate but remember a $25 parking fee. That one charge can make the whole stay feel expensive.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the signpost is usually the entry plan price that review sites and comparison tables quote. Buyers often judge your whole pricing from that one number.

cards.title: A cheap signpost needs a business behind it.
body: Costco can hold the hot dog at $1.50 partly because much of its profit comes from membership fees. Those do go up: the basic US membership rose from $60 to $65 in 2024.
A cheap item with nothing to pay for it is just a loss. And a famous frozen price becomes a promise. The longer you hold it, the more trust a future increase will cost.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your team-chat app has three plans. The $8 starter plan hasn't changed in five years, and it's the price every review site quotes. Hosting and support costs are up.

options.feedback: Simple, even-handed, and it covers costs. But it moves the one number people use to judge you, so the story becomes "price hike."

options.text: Keep the $8 starter plan and raise the higher plans, where heavy users are
options.feedback: You protect the price everyone quotes and recover costs where usage is highest. The trade-off: bigger customers may push back, so show them what they get.

options.text: Keep $8 but quietly cut what the starter plan includes
options.feedback: The headline survives, but users and reviewers notice a smaller plan quickly. It reads as a hidden price rise and hurts your price image more than an honest one.

cards.softwareNote: Look at which price shows up in reviews, ads and comparison sites. That's your hot dog.

cards.title: Some prices are signs, not just prices.
body: Customers judge your whole business from the few prices they remember. Protect those, and earn your margin elsewhere.
**Try it today:** ask three customers what anything at your business costs. The prices they can name without looking are your signposts.
